# --- Baseline: the rules working as advertised ------------------------------
# A single star stays inside one segment.
# ... and does not leak into the parent segment either.
# ** is a whole segment and spans zero or more of them.
# ** in the middle of a pattern.
# ? is exactly one byte, and never the separator.
# Character classes, including the POSIX literal-']'-first rule.
# Classic .. traversal. The path is unresolved, so it is not a mismatch, it is
# a case the validator must not answer at all.
# Doubled and disguised forms. "..." and ".." inside a segment name are just
# filenames; only a bare ".." segment is traversal.
# A single "." segment is equally unresolved: something skipped normalization.
# An empty segment means an unnormalized path reached the matcher.
# URL-encoded traversal. %2e%2e is a filename to the kernel, never traversal,
# so this must match the subtree rather than being read as an escape.
# Relative paths never match anything: the resolver failed or the probe
# truncated, and an unresolved path is not a safe path.
# A path truncated at ALLSEER_PATH_MAX mid-segment still looks well-formed. It
# matches the pattern it was truncated into, which is exactly why truncation
# must be flagged as an enrichment failure upstream and never reach here.
# A sibling directory sharing the root's name prefix is not inside the root.
# A pattern must not match a longer path just because it is a prefix of one.
# Dotfiles are ordinary. This is the decision that makes a denial of /ws/**
# actually cover /ws/.env; a shell-style "* skips dotfiles" rule would leave
# every credential file in the workspace outside every denial.
# Matching is byte-exact, so case matters even when the host filesystem's does
# not. On a case-insensitive filesystem a denial can be evaded by case; that is
# a documented limitation, not a matcher bug.
# A directory is the same directory however it is spelled.
# ** only means anything as a whole segment; mixing is rejected rather than
# quietly demoted to * (too narrow) or promoted to a subtree (too wide).
